 Singapore Moves to Strengthen Haze Law. Will Malaysia Finally Act?
 Greenpeace Malaysia
 October 29, 2026 
 • 
 2 min read
 • 
 0 Comments 
 Share on Whatsapp 
 Share on Facebook

 Share via Email 
 Share on Bluesky 
 Add as a preferred source on Google 
 Versi Bahasa Malaysia 
 KUALA LUMPUR, 29 October 2026 – As Singapore moves to strengthen its transboundary haze law and investigate potential corporate links to haze in Indonesia, Greenpeace Malaysia is urging the Malaysian government to follow suit by introducing a Clean Air Act with strong transboundary provisions.
 Singapore recently announced plans to address enforcement gaps in its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, particularly challenges in obtaining evidence and securing corporate cooperation across borders. On 28 October, Singapore’s senior government leaders met representatives of 10 Singapore-based companies to seek their cooperation with investigations. Proposed amendments would strengthen requirements for independent assessments of corporate operations, ownership structures and supply chains, backed by penalties for non-compliance.
 Greenpeace Malaysia Interim Country Representative Heng Kiah Chun said: 
 “ Singapore is not just questioning companies. It is taking steps to close enforcement gaps in its haze law. Malaysia has cited similar challenges as obstacles to stronger legislation. If Singapore is taking action to address them, why can’t Malaysia do the same? Haze crosses borders. Corporate accountability must too. 
 Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has previously pledged that Malaysia would not shield companies found responsible for forest and land fires in Indonesia. However, the Malaysian government maintains that there is no conclusive evidence linking Malaysian companies to the fires. Plantation and Commodities Minister Datuk Seri Dr Noraini Ahmad recently stated that fires originated outside Malaysian-owned plantation areas, while Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Minister Datuk Seri Arthur Joseph Kurup reiterated in Parliament that no conclusive evidence had been established against Malaysian-linked companies, following concerns raised by Indonesian environmental organisation WALHI.”
 “If the government maintains that there is no conclusive evidence linking Malaysian companies to the fires in Indonesia, it should make the evidence and findings behind that conclusion public. Transparency and independent scrutiny are essential to establishing the facts and protecting responsible businesses.” – Heng added. 
 The need for greater scrutiny is also highlighted in a joint report released by Greenpeace and Pantau Gambut on 5 October. Titled When Clean Air Is Sacrificed for Global Commodities , the report identified 20 forestry and palm oil concession entities associated with haze-source points in Indonesia, including concessions connected to Malaysian and Singaporean business interests. While these findings do not establish corporate responsibility, they warrant further independent scrutiny.
 Greenpeace Malaysia reiterates that a Clean Air Act with strong transboundary provisions is not anti-business. It is pro-responsible business. Stronger legislation would help Malaysia obtain corporate information, investigate ownership structures, supply chains and hold those found responsible accountable. It would also give companies wrongly implicated a credible way to clear their names.
